---
title: "Module 3 — Organising quantitative data: histograms and cumulative curves"
subtitle: "Data Description | Part I — Organising data"
date-modified: 2026-10-18
---

**The business question.** The owner of the Harbour truck is planning
how much food to prepare. Each day brings a different revenue, to the
cent, so a list of 30 or 120 numbers tells her nothing at a glance. How
is daily revenue *distributed*? Are most days clustered around €600, or
spread all over the place? And on how many days do we earn less than
€500? This module turns a long column of continuous numbers into a
short table and three pictures that answer these questions. We start
with five days, small enough to sort by hand, and only then write the
formulas.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Explain why a continuous variable must be grouped into classes before
  it can be summarised in a frequency table.
- Choose a sensible number of classes and a class width, and write the
  classes with the half-open convention $[L_i, L_i + h[$.
- Build a class table with counts, relative frequencies and cumulative
  frequencies, by hand and in Excel.
- Draw and read a histogram, a frequency polygon and a cumulative
  frequency curve, including a histogram with unequal class widths.
- Read a percentile or a share of observations off the cumulative curve.
- Read the symbols $n_i$, $f_i$, $N_i^{+}$ and $F_i^{+}$ aloud as
  sentences, and write them from a description in words.

## Theory

### Five days, five different numbers

Here is the daily revenue of a Harbour-style truck over five days. The
numbers are a simplified extract chosen so that you can do everything by
hand.

| Day | Revenue (€) |
|---|---:|
| 1 | 600 |
| 2 | 470 |
| 3 | 730 |
| 4 | 550 |
| 5 | 430 |

All five revenues are different, so a frequency table like the ones of
[Module 2](module-02.qmd) would have five rows, each with a count of 1.
With 120 days recorded to the cent it would be 120 rows: as long as the
data. How would you summarise these five days in three or four lines, so
that the owner sees at a glance where most days sit?

### Classes: grouping a continuous variable

**Try it.** Cut the revenue axis into classes of width 100 starting at
400, and put each day into its class. Be careful with Day 1, which
earned exactly €600.

| Class (€) | Days in the class | Count |
|---|---|---:|
| [400, 500[ | ? | ? |
| [500, 600[ | ? | ? |
| [600, 700[ | ? | ? |
| [700, 800[ | ? | ? |
| **Total** | | **?** |

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Class (€) | Days in the class | Count |
|---|---|---:|
| [400, 500[ | Day 2 (470), Day 5 (430) | 2 |
| [500, 600[ | Day 4 (550) | 1 |
| [600, 700[ | Day 1 (600) | 1 |
| [700, 800[ | Day 3 (730) | 1 |
| **Total** | | **5** |

Day 1 (exactly 600) goes into [600, 700[: the lower bound belongs to the
class. The counts add up to 5, so no day was lost or counted twice.

</details>

**See it.** Each cross is one day on the revenue axis; the bars of the
axis mark the class bounds. Day 1 sits exactly on the bound 600.

```text
400       500       600       700       800
|---------|---------|---------|---------|
   x   x       x    x            x
```

In plain words: a class table trades precision for readability. You
lose the exact values, but you can finally *see* where the data sit.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — class (grouped) frequency table
When almost every value of a continuous variable is different, a plain
frequency table lists each value once and says nothing useful. The fix
is to cut the range of values into $k$ consecutive **classes**
(intervals) of width $h$ and count how many observations fall into each
one. Classes are written **half-open**, $[L_i, L_i + h[$: the lower
bound belongs to the class, the upper bound belongs to the next class.
So every value lands in exactly one class.
:::

### How many classes, how wide?

**Try it.** For our five days ($n = 5$, minimum 430, maximum 730),
find the number of classes and the width that Sturges' rule suggests.
Use $\log_{10}(5) \approx 0.699$.

| Step | Value |
|---|---:|
| $k \approx 1 + 3.3 \times 0.699$ | ? |
| Range $= \text{max} - \text{min}$ | ? |
| $h \approx \text{range} / k$ | ? |
| $h$ rounded to a convenient number | ? |

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Step | Value |
|---|---:|
| $k \approx 1 + 3.3 \times 0.699$ | 3.3 |
| Range $= \text{max} - \text{min}$ | 300 |
| $h \approx \text{range} / k$ | about 91 |
| $h$ rounded to a convenient number | 100 |

Starting at a round number at or below 430, that is 400, classes of
width 100 give the four classes you used above.

</details>

**See it.** The same range of 300 euros cut in three ways:

| Width $h$ | Classes | What the table shows |
|---:|---:|---|
| 300 | 1 | everything in one class: the shape is hidden |
| 100 | 4 | counts 2, 1, 1, 1: a readable summary |
| 25 | 12 | five classes hold one day each, the rest are empty: noise |

In plain words: more data can support more classes, but slowly. Thirty
days give about 6 classes; 120 days give about 8. Too few classes hide
the shape; too many make a ragged picture where each bar holds only one
or two days.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Rule of thumb — Sturges' rule
For $n$ observations, a good number of classes is about
$$
k \approx 1 + 3.3 \log_{10}(n),
\qquad
h \approx \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{k},
$$
then round $h$ to a convenient number (10, 50, 100 …) and start the
first class at a round number at or below the minimum.
:::

#### Notation decoder: Sturges' rule

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (five days) |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | "n" | 5 days |
| $k$ | "k" | the number of classes, about 3.3 |
| $\log_{10}(n)$ | "log base ten of n" | $\log_{10}(5) \approx 0.699$ |
| $\text{max}$, $\text{min}$ | "the maximum, the minimum" | 730 and 430 |
| $h$ | "h" | the class width, about 91, rounded to 100 |
| $\approx$ | "is about" | the rule gives a guide, not an exact answer |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the number of classes is about one plus
3.3 times the base-ten logarithm of the number of observations; the
class width is about the range divided by that number of classes."

For the first 30 Harbour days, revenue runs from €407.59 to €886.56, a
range of €478.97. Sturges gives $k \approx 5.9$ and $h \approx 82$, which
we round to **$h = 100$** with the first class starting at 400. That
gives five classes.

### Frequencies in a class table

**Try it.** Complete the class table of the five days
($n = 5$). Fill each column from left to right.

| Class (€) | $n_i$ | $N_i^{+}$ | $f_i$ (%) | $F_i^{+}$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 2 | ? | ? | ? |
| [500, 600[ | 1 | ? | ? | ? |
| [600, 700[ | 1 | ? | ? | ? |
| [700, 800[ | 1 | ? | ? | ? |

1. $N_i^{+}$: the running total of the counts.
2. $f_i$: each count divided by $n = 5$, as a percentage.
3. $F_i^{+}$: the running total divided by $n = 5$.

How many days earned less than €700?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Class (€) | $n_i$ | $N_i^{+}$ | $f_i$ (%) | $F_i^{+}$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 2 | 2 | 40 | 40 |
| [500, 600[ | 1 | 3 | 20 | 60 |
| [600, 700[ | 1 | 4 | 20 | 80 |
| [700, 800[ | 1 | 5 | 20 | 100 |

Less than €700 means the first three classes: $N_3^{+} = 4$ days, that
is $F_3^{+} = 80\%$. The last row always ends at $n = 5$ and 100%.

</details>

**See it.** The running totals grow like a staircase that stops at $n$:

```text
less than 500   ##        2 days   40%
less than 600   ###       3 days   60%
less than 700   ####      4 days   80%
less than 800   #####     5 days  100%
```

In plain words: $n_i$ is a count; $f_i$ is its share of the total (often
written as a percentage); $N_i^{+}$ and $F_i^{+}$ are the running totals
of counts and shares up to and including class $i$. The last one answers
"how many days earned **less than the upper bound** of this class?".

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formulas — counts, shares and running totals
For class $i$, with $n_i$ the number of observations in it and $n$ the
total number of observations:
$$
f_i = \frac{n_i}{n},
\qquad
N_i^{+} = \sum_{j=1}^{i} n_j,
\qquad
F_i^{+} = \frac{N_i^{+}}{n}.
$$
:::

#### Notation decoder: counts, shares and running totals

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (five days) |
|---|---|---|
| $i$ | "i" | the class number, 1 to 4 |
| $n_i$ | "n sub i" | the count of class $i$, e.g. $n_1 = 2$ |
| $n$ | "n" | the total, 5 days |
| $f_i$ | "f sub i" | the share of class $i$, e.g. $f_1 = 2/5 = 40\%$ |
| $\sum_{j=1}^{i}$ | "add up, for j from 1 to i" | for $i = 3$: $2 + 1 + 1$ |
| $n_j$ | "n sub j" | the count of class $j$ |
| $N_i^{+}$ | "capital N sub i plus" | the days below the upper bound of class $i$, e.g. $N_3^{+} = 4$ |
| $F_i^{+}$ | "capital F sub i plus" | the share of days below that bound, e.g. $F_3^{+} = 4/5 = 80\%$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the share of a class is its count
divided by the total; the cumulative count of a class is the sum of the
counts of all classes up to and including it; the cumulative share is
that cumulative count divided by the total."

### The histogram

**Try it.** The last two classes of the five-day table are merged into
one class [600, 800[. Complete the table, then decide which bar is the
tallest if you draw **heights** and which if you want **areas**
proportional to the counts.

| Class (€) | Width $h_i$ | $n_i$ | Raw count | $n_i / h_i$ (days per €) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 100 | 2 | 2 | ? |
| [500, 600[ | 100 | 1 | 1 | ? |
| [600, 800[ | 200 | ? | ? | ? |

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

| Class (€) | Width $h_i$ | $n_i$ | Raw count | $n_i / h_i$ (days per €) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 100 | 2 | 2 | 0.02 |
| [500, 600[ | 100 | 1 | 1 | 0.01 |
| [600, 800[ | 200 | 2 | 2 | 0.01 |

With raw counts, [600, 800[ would look as tall as [400, 500[ although it
is twice as wide, so its area would be doubled. With the density it is
drawn at 0.01, half the height of the first bar: the areas
$100 \times 0.02 = 2$ and $200 \times 0.01 = 2$ are equal, as the counts
are.

</details>

**See it.** In the figure below, choose **1 · Histogram**: the bars
touch, and the height of each bar is the count of the class. The next
section uses the other two views of the same figure.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
miniRevenue = [600, 470, 730, 550, 430]

viewof miniView = {
  const labels = ["1 · Histogram", "2 · Polygon", "3 · Cumulative curve"];
  const form = html`<form class="ojs-step-picker">Show: ${labels.map((l, i) =>
    html`<label> <input type="radio" name="mini-view" value="${i + 1}"
      ${i === 0 ? "checked" : ""}> ${l} </label>`)}</form>`;
  form.value = 1;
  form.oninput = () => {
    form.value = +form.querySelector("input:checked").value;
  };
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const xs = miniRevenue, n = xs.length;
  const lo = 400, h = 100, k = 4;
  const counts = Array.from({length: k}, (_, i) =>
    xs.filter(v => v >= lo + i * h && v < lo + (i + 1) * h).length);
  const cum = [];
  counts.reduce((acc, c) => { cum.push(acc + c); return acc + c; }, 0);
  const share = cum.map(c => 100 * c / n);
  const W = 660, H = 320, L = 60, R = 20, T = 30, B = 50;
  const BLUE = "steelblue", ORANGE = "darkorange";
  const x = v => L + (v - lo) * (W - L - R) / (k * h);
  const cmax = Math.max(...counts);
  const yc = c => H - B - c * (H - T - B) / cmax;
  const yp = p => H - B - p * (H - T - B) / 100;
  let g = "";

  const cumView = miniView === 3;
  const ticks = cumView ? [0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100]
                        : Array.from({length: cmax + 1}, (_, c) => c);
  ticks.forEach(t => {
    const y = cumView ? yp(t) : yc(t);
    g += `<line x1="${L}" x2="${W - R}" y1="${y}" y2="${y}"
      stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.15"/>
      <text x="${L - 8}" y="${y + 4}" text-anchor="end"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">${t}${cumView ? "%" : ""}</text>`;
  });
  for (let v = lo; v <= lo + k * h; v += h) {
    g += `<text x="${x(v)}" y="${H - B + 18}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">${v}</text>`;
  }
  g += `<text x="${W / 2}" y="${H - 8}" text-anchor="middle"
    fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Daily revenue (EUR)</text>`;

  let caption = "";
  if (miniView < 3) {
    counts.forEach((c, i) => {
      g += `<rect x="${x(lo + i * h)}" y="${yc(c)}" width="${x(lo + (i + 1) * h) - x(lo + i * h)}"
        height="${yc(0) - yc(c)}" fill="${BLUE}"
        fill-opacity="${miniView === 1 ? 0.85 : 0.3}" stroke="${BLUE}"/>`;
    });
    if (miniView === 2) {
      const pts = counts.map((c, i) => [lo + (i + 0.5) * h, c]);
      g += `<polyline fill="none" stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2"
        points="${pts.map(([a, c]) => `${x(a)},${yc(c)}`).join(" ")}"/>`;
      pts.forEach(([a, c]) => {
        g += `<circle cx="${x(a)}" cy="${yc(c)}" r="5" fill="${ORANGE}"/>`;
      });
    }
    g += `<text x="14" y="${H / 2}" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 14 ${H / 2})">Number of days</text>`;
    caption = miniView === 1
      ? `Counts ${counts.join(", ")}: they add up to ${counts.reduce((a, c) => a + c, 0)} days.`
      : `Polygon points (midpoint, count): ${counts.map((c, i) =>
          `(${lo + (i + 0.5) * h}, ${c})`).join(", ")}.`;
  } else {
    const pts = [[lo, 0], ...share.map((p, i) => [lo + (i + 1) * h, p])];
    g += `<polyline fill="none" stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2"
      points="${pts.map(([a, p]) => `${x(a)},${yp(p)}`).join(" ")}"/>`;
    pts.forEach(([a, p]) => {
      g += `<circle cx="${x(a)}" cy="${yp(p)}" r="5" fill="${ORANGE}"/>`;
    });
    const i = share.findIndex(p => p >= 50);
    const prev = i === 0 ? 0 : share[i - 1];
    const x50 = lo + i * h + h * (50 - prev) / (share[i] - prev);
    g += `<line x1="${L}" x2="${x(x50)}" y1="${yp(50)}" y2="${yp(50)}"
      stroke="${BLUE}" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="2"/>
      <line x1="${x(x50)}" x2="${x(x50)}" y1="${yp(50)}" y2="${yp(0)}"
      stroke="${BLUE}" stroke-dasharray="5 4" stroke-width="2"/>`;
    g += `<text x="14" y="${H / 2}" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 14 ${H / 2})">Share of days below</text>`;
    caption = `Points (upper bound, share): ${share.map((p, j) =>
      `(${lo + (j + 1) * h}, ${p}%)`).join(", ")}. The curve crosses 50%
      at about ${x50}.`;
  }
  return html`<div><svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Histogram, polygon and cumulative curve of five daily revenues">
    ${g}</svg><p><em>${caption}</em></p></div>`;
}
```

In plain words: your eye reads *area*, not height. A wide class holds
more days than a narrow one of the same height, so for unequal widths we
divide the count by the width to keep the picture honest.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — histogram
A **histogram** draws one rectangle per class, with the rectangles
touching each other (the variable is continuous, so there are no gaps).
The **area** of a rectangle is proportional to the number of
observations in the class. When all classes have the same width $h$,
area is proportional to height, so the height is simply $n_i$. When the
widths differ, the height must be the **density**
$$
\text{height}_i = \frac{n_i}{h_i}.
$$
:::

### Frequency polygon and cumulative curve

**Try it.** From the five-day table, write the point that the
frequency polygon plots for the class [500, 600[, and the point that the
cumulative curve plots at the end of that class. Then read the curve at
$p = 50\%$: it crosses 50% between 500 (40%) and 600 (60%), so by how
much has it climbed from 500 when it reaches 50%?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Check your answer</summary>

- Polygon: the midpoint is $(500 + 600)/2 = 550$ and $n_2 = 1$, so the
  point is **(550, 1)**.
- Cumulative curve: the **upper bound** against the running share,
  **(600, 60%)**.
- Between (500, 40%) and (600, 60%), 50% is halfway up the segment
  ($10$ out of $20$ points), so the reading is $500 + 100 \times
  \frac{10}{20} = 550$. Half of the five days earned less than about
  €550.

</details>

**See it.** In the figure above, choose **2 · Polygon** to see the
midpoints joined by lines, then **3 · Cumulative curve** to see the
upper bounds against the running share, with the 50% reading dashed.

- The **frequency polygon** joins the points (class midpoint, $n_i$)
  with straight lines. It carries the same information as the histogram
  but is easier to superimpose for two distributions.
- The **cumulative frequency curve** (also called the *ogive*) joins the
  points (class **upper bound**, $F_i^{+}$) and starts at $0\%$ on the
  lower bound of the first class. It never goes down and ends at $100\%$.

In plain words: inside a class we assume the observations are spread
evenly, so the curve is a straight line there. Find the class where the
curve crosses $p$, then move along that straight segment.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — reading a percentile on the cumulative curve
If the share $p$ you are looking for lies between $F_{i-1}^{+}$ and
$F_i^{+}$ in class $[L_i, L_i + h[$, linear interpolation gives
$$
x_p \approx L_i + h \times
\frac{p - F_{i-1}^{+}}{F_i^{+} - F_{i-1}^{+}}.
$$
:::

#### Notation decoder: reading a percentile on the cumulative curve

| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (five days, $p = 50\%$) |
|---|---|---|
| $p$ | "p" | the share we look for, 50% |
| $i$ | "i" | the class where the curve crosses $p$: class 2, [500, 600[ |
| $L_i$ | "L sub i" | the lower bound of that class, 500 |
| $h$ | "h" | the class width, 100 |
| $F_{i-1}^{+}$ | "capital F sub i minus one, plus" | the share before the class, 40% |
| $F_i^{+}$ | "capital F sub i plus" | the share at its upper bound, 60% |
| $x_p$ | "x sub p" | the revenue below which a share $p$ of days lie, about 550 |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "start at the lower bound of the class
where the curve crosses $p$, and add the class width multiplied by the
fraction of the way that $p$ lies between the shares at the two ends of
the class."

## Worked example

We use the **first 30 trading days of Harbour** (sheet `harbour_30d`).
The class table for `daily_revenue_eur` with $h = 100$ and $n = 30$ is:

| Class (€) | $n_i$ | $N_i^{+}$ | $f_i$ (%) | $F_i^{+}$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 6 | 6 | 20.0 | 20.0 |
| [500, 600[ | 6 | 12 | 20.0 | 40.0 |
| [600, 700[ | 8 | 20 | 26.7 | 66.7 |
| [700, 800[ | 7 | 27 | 23.3 | 90.0 |
| [800, 900[ | 3 | 30 | 10.0 | 100.0 |

**Step 1 — the histogram.** All five classes have width 100, so the bar
heights are the counts 6, 6, 8, 7, 3. The tallest bar is [600, 700[:
that is where the largest group of trading days sits.

**Step 2 — the frequency polygon.** The class midpoints are
450, 550, 650, 750 and 850. Plot (450, 6), (550, 6), (650, 8), (750, 7),
(850, 3) and join them with straight lines.

**Step 3 — the cumulative curve.** Plot the upper bounds against
$F_i^{+}$: (500, 20%), (600, 40%), (700, 66.7%), (800, 90%),
(900, 100%), starting from (400, 0%). Reading at 600 tells us that
**40%** of the days earned less than €600.

**Step 4 — reading the curve.** Where does the curve cross 50%? Between
600 (40%) and 700 (66.7%), so
$$
x_{50} \approx 600 + 100 \times \frac{50 - 40}{66.7 - 40} \approx 637.5.
$$
The exact median of the 30 values is €643.63, so the curve reading is
within €6. For the third quartile, $p = 75\%$ lies between 700 (66.7%)
and 800 (90%): $x_{75} \approx 700 + 100 \times
\frac{75 - 66.7}{90 - 66.7} \approx 735.7$ (the exact value, computed in
Module 5, is €729.99).


**Exam tip.** A cumulative curve is read at **upper bounds**. A polygon
is read at **midpoints**. Mixing them up is the most common error on
this topic.

## Proof / derivation

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — the cumulative curve must reach 100% (click to expand)
By definition $N_k^{+} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} n_j$, summed over **all** $k$
classes. The classes are consecutive and half-open, so every observation
falls in exactly one class and the class counts add up to the total:
$$
N_k^{+} = \sum_{j=1}^{k} n_j = n
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
F_k^{+} = \frac{N_k^{+}}{n} = \frac{n}{n} = 100\%.
$$
For the first 30 Harbour days, $N_5^{+} = 6+6+8+7+3 = 30 = n$, so
$F_5^{+} = 100\%$. Whatever class bounds you choose, the cumulative
curve always finishes in the top-right corner. If it does not, a class
is missing or an observation fell outside your classes — a quick way to
check your own table.
:::

## Visual intuition

Think of the histogram as a **pile of sand** poured on the revenue axis.
The area of each bar is the amount of sand in that class, and the total
area is the whole sample (the 30 days). If every class has the same
width, a taller bar means more sand. If a class is twice as wide and you
keep the same height, you have silently doubled its sand: the picture
lies. Dividing the count by the width ($n_i/h_i$) keeps the amount of
sand honest.

The cumulative curve is the same pile seen from another angle: at any
revenue $x$, its height is the share of sand lying to the **left** of
$x$. Where the histogram has a tall bar, the curve climbs steeply; where
the histogram is nearly empty, the curve is nearly flat.

```{ojs}
    657.88, 67.08, 474.32, 607.24, 178.05, 346.90, 317.60, 208.79,
    331.38, 315.26, 335.38, 273.53, 227.29, 187.58, 620.20, 116.27
  ];
  const CAMPUS_120 = [
    1089.40, 1335.48, 540.03, 598.76, 377.74, 170.84, 23.85, 368.83,
    599.66, 432.71, 478.40, 572.40, 299.09, 186.26, 556.11, 356.11,
    658.89, 697.39, 361.09, 277.62, 172.24, 870.03, 1407.59, 448.33,
    715.64, 267.68, 114.21, 323.14, 396.69, 742.01, 1114.89, 741.91,
    275.82, 245.21, 55.06, 346.24, 598.12, 989.43, 295.85, 138.44,
    267.00, 72.34, 898.08, 384.09, 291.95, 472.05, 667.05, 79.47,
    26.57, 1135.89, 951.18, 403.89, 427.84, 156.30, 181.88, 30.58,
    241.99, 380.60, 318.68, 446.42, 413.63, 159.43, 121.60, 577.01,
    493.92, 436.74, 529.14, 524.11, 35.80, 234.09, 359.34, 269.31,
    246.10, 270.87, 747.84, 436.33, 180.67, 402.41, 348.79, 717.81,
    399.38, 864.08, 171.61, 213.40, 333.03, 566.94, 519.92, 439.65,
    568.41, 251.73, 49.02, 950.12, 345.89, 569.65, 483.54, 251.10,
    227.23, 198.44, 849.86, 1000.56, 621.45, 441.41, 574.90, 93.29,
    204.87, 521.04, 268.06, 859.15, 949.10, 175.90, 179.84, 208.10,
    1062.98, 761.06, 773.08, 278.86, 245.06, 127.26, 63.49, 1362.93
  ];
  const DATASETS = {
    harbour30: ["Harbour, first 30 days", HARBOUR_120.slice(0, 30)],
    harbour120: ["Harbour, all 120 days", HARBOUR_120],
    campus120: ["Campus, all 120 days", CAMPUS_120]
  };
  const root = html`<div class="ojs-demo">
    <form>
      <p>Data:
        <label><input type="radio" name="hist-data" value="harbour30" checked>
          Harbour, first 30 days</label>
        <label><input type="radio" name="hist-data" value="harbour120">
          Harbour, all 120 days</label>
        <label><input type="radio" name="hist-data" value="campus120">
          Campus, all 120 days</label>
      </p>
      <label>Bin width (EUR):
        <input type="range" name="width" min="25" max="400" step="25"
          value="100"> <output>100</output></label>
    </form>
    <p class="ojs-demo-info"></p>
    <div class="ojs-demo-chart"></div>
  </div>`;
  const form = root.querySelector("form");

  function redraw() {
    const key = form.querySelector("input[name=hist-data]:checked").value;
    const [label, values] = DATASETS[key];
    const w = +form.querySelector("input[name=width]").value;
    form.querySelector("output").textContent = w;
    const n = values.length, vmin = Math.min(...values), vmax = Math.max(...values);
    const lo = Math.floor(vmin / w) * w;
    const hi = (Math.floor(vmax / w) + 1) * w;
    const k = Math.round((hi - lo) / w);
    const counts = new Array(k).fill(0);
    values.forEach(v => { counts[Math.min(k - 1, Math.floor((v - lo) / w))] += 1; });
    const sturges = 1 + 3.3 * Math.log10(n);
    const suggested = (vmax - vmin) / sturges;
    root.querySelector(".ojs-demo-info").innerHTML =
      `n = <strong>${n}</strong> days · bin width = <strong>${w}</strong> EUR
       → <strong>${k}</strong> classes<br>Sturges suggests about
       ${sturges.toFixed(1)} classes, i.e. a width near
       ${suggested.toFixed(0)} EUR.`;

    const W = 660, Ht = 340, L = 50, R = 15, T = 30, B = 45;
    const cmax = Math.max(...counts);
    const x = v => L + (v - lo) * (W - L - R) / (hi - lo);
    const y = c => Ht - B - c * (Ht - T - B) / cmax;
    let g = `<text x="${W / 2}" y="18" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="14">${label}</text>`;
    const step = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(cmax / 6));
    for (let c = 0; c <= cmax; c += step) {
      g += `<line x1="${L}" x2="${W - R}" y1="${y(c)}" y2="${y(c)}"
        stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.15"/>
        <text x="${L - 6}" y="${y(c) + 4}" text-anchor="end"
        fill="currentColor" font-size="11">${c}</text>`;
    }
    counts.forEach((c, i) => {
      const x0 = x(lo + i * w), x1 = x(lo + (i + 1) * w);
      g += `<rect x="${x0}" y="${y(c)}" width="${Math.max(0, x1 - x0 - 1)}"
        height="${y(0) - y(c)}" fill="steelblue" fill-opacity="0.9"/>`;
    });
    const tick = Math.ceil((hi - lo) / w / 8) * w;
    for (let v = lo; v <= hi; v += tick) {
      g += `<text x="${x(v)}" y="${Ht - B + 16}" text-anchor="middle"
        fill="currentColor" font-size="11">${v}</text>`;
    }
    g += `<text x="${W / 2}" y="${Ht - 6}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Daily revenue (EUR)</text>
      <text x="14" y="${Ht / 2}" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 14 ${Ht / 2})">Number of days</text>`;
    root.querySelector(".ojs-demo-chart").innerHTML =
      `<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${Ht}" width="100%" role="img"
        aria-label="Histogram of daily revenue">${g}</svg>`;
  }
  form.addEventListener("input", redraw);
  redraw();
  return root;
}
```

## Exercises

All exercises below are done by hand; the Excel ones are in the
[homework](#homework-excel-lab).

::: {#exr-reading-cumulative-curve name="Reading the cumulative curve"}
Use the worked-example table (Harbour, first 30 days). What percentage
of trading days earned **at least** €700?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The curve gives $F^{+}(700) = 66.7\%$ of days **below**
€700, so at least €700 means
$100\% - 66.7\% = 33.3\%$. Check with the counts directly:
$(7 + 3)/30 = 33.3\%$.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-unequal-class-widths name="Unequal class widths"}
Suppose the last two classes are merged into one class [700, 900[ of
width 200, which holds $7 + 3 = 10$ days. The first class [400, 500[ has
width 100 and holds 6 days. What heights should the two bars have so
that their **areas** are comparable? Which bar looks taller?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Use the density $n_i/h_i$.

- [400, 500[: $6/100 = 0.06$ days per euro.
- [700, 900[: $10/200 = 0.05$ days per euro.

The merged bar is drawn at height $0.05$ — about 83% of the height of
the first bar, even though it holds more days (10 versus 6), because it
is twice as wide. Had we plotted the raw count 10, the merged class
would look almost twice as tall as it should.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-polygon-points name="Polygon points"}
What is the midpoint of the class [600, 700[, and which point does the
frequency polygon plot for it? What is the point for the cumulative
curve at the end of that class?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The midpoint is $(600 + 700)/2 = 650$ and
$n_{[600,700[} = 8$, so the polygon plots **(650, 8)**. The cumulative
curve plots the **upper bound** against the running share:
**(700, 66.7%)**.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-formula-words name="Formula to words"}
(a) Read $F_i^{+} = \dfrac{N_i^{+}}{n}$ aloud as one sentence. Which
indicator is it?

(b) Read $N_i^{+} = \sum_{j=1}^{i} n_j$ aloud as one sentence. For the
five-day table of the Theory section, what is $N_3^{+}$?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) "The cumulative share of class $i$ is the cumulative count of class
$i$ divided by the total number of observations." It is the share of
days below the upper bound of class $i$.

(b) "The cumulative count of class $i$ is the sum, for $j$ from 1 to
$i$, of the counts of the classes." For the five days,
$N_3^{+} = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4$.

</details>
:::

::: {#exr-words-formula name="Words to formula"}
Write in symbols: (a) "the share of the observations that fall in class
$i$"; (b) "the height of the bar of class $i$ when the class widths
differ"; (c) "the revenue below which a share $p$ of the days lie,
read on the cumulative curve inside the class $[L_i, L_i + h[$".

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

(a) $f_i = \dfrac{n_i}{n}$.

(b) $\text{height}_i = \dfrac{n_i}{h_i}$.

(c) $x_p \approx L_i + h \times
\dfrac{p - F_{i-1}^{+}}{F_i^{+} - F_{i-1}^{+}}$.

</details>
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Watch out
- **Plotting the raw count for unequal widths.** Use the density
  $n_i/h_i$, otherwise wide classes look too large.
- **Mixing up the plotting positions.** Polygon points use the class
  **midpoint**; the cumulative curve uses the class **upper bound**.
- **Overlapping or gappy classes.** Write them half-open, $[L, L+h[$, so
  each value belongs to exactly one class.
- **Too few or too many classes.** Two classes hide the shape; 40 classes
  on 30 observations draw noise. Start from Sturges' rule and adjust.
- **Leaving gaps between histogram bars.** The variable is continuous:
  bars touch. Gaps belong to bar charts of *categories* (Module 2).
:::


## Exit check

Five minutes, no calculator needed except for question 4.

1. In one sentence, why must a continuous variable be grouped into
   classes before building a frequency table?
2. Why are the bounds of a class written $[L_i, L_i + h[$, with the
   upper bound left out?
3. Read $F_i^{+} = N_i^{+}/n$ aloud as a sentence.
4. A class table of $n = 10$ days has counts 3, 5 and 2 in the classes
   [0, 200[, [200, 400[ and [400, 600[. What are $f_2$ and the
   cumulative share $F_2^{+}$?
5. Which points does a frequency polygon use, and which does a
   cumulative curve use? Why are they different?

<details class="answer">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Almost every value is different, so a table by value would be as long
   as the data; classes trade a little precision for a readable summary.
2. So that every value lands in exactly one class: the lower bound
   belongs to the class, the upper bound belongs to the next one.
3. "The cumulative share of class $i$ is the cumulative count of class
   $i$ divided by the total number of observations."
4. $f_2 = 5/10 = 50\%$ and $F_2^{+} = (3 + 5)/10 = 80\%$.
5. The polygon uses (class midpoint, count): it describes the class as a
   whole. The cumulative curve uses (class upper bound, cumulative
   share): the share of days below a bound is only known once the whole
   class has been counted.

</details>

## Homework — Excel lab

Reproduce, in Excel, every table you built by hand in class, with
`COUNTIFS` and a running sum, then apply them to the full dataset.

**Estimated time:** about 50–60 minutes. Any spreadsheet application
works, at home or in a campus computer room.

**Follow-up:** a 10-minute debrief at the start of
[Module 4](module-04.qmd). Bring your Step 0 results and any question on
Homework 1–2.

### Using Excel

The sheet `harbour_30d` of `wandering-fork.xlsx` has the same 16 columns
as the main table; `daily_revenue_eur` is column N, rows 2 to 31. The
complete list of function names, with their French equivalents, is on
the [Excel functions](excel-functions.qmd) page.

| Concept | Excel function or steps |
|---|---|
| Class bounds | Type the lower bounds 400, 500, … in column R and the upper bounds in column S (each upper bound is the next lower bound) |
| Count $n_i$ (column T) | `=COUNTIFS($N$2:$N$31,">="&R2,$N$2:$N$31,"<"&S2)`, then copy down |
| Relative frequency $f_i$ (column U) | `=T2/COUNT($N$2:$N$31)`, formatted as a percentage |
| Cumulative count $N_i^{+}$ (column V) | In the first row `=T2`; below, `=V2+T3` (running sum), then copy down |
| Cumulative share $F_i^{+}$ (column W) | `=V2/COUNT($N$2:$N$31)`, formatted as a percentage |
| Same count in one step | `=COUNTIFS($N$2:$N$31,"<"&S2)` gives $N_i^{+}$ directly |
| Histogram | Select the revenue column → **Insert → Chart → Histogram**, then **Format Axis → Bin width** = 100 |
| PivotTable grouping | Insert a PivotTable, put `daily_revenue_eur` in **Rows** and `day` in **Values** (Count), then right-click a row → **Group** with *Starting at* 400, *Ending at* 900, *By* 100 |
| Frequency polygon | **Insert → Chart → Line** (or Scatter with straight lines) using the midpoints and counts |
| Cumulative curve | **Insert → Chart → Scatter with Straight Lines** using the upper bounds and $F_i^{+}$ |

For the **full table** (120 days per franchise) use the Excel Table
`tblFork` and add the franchise as one more condition, for example:

```text
=COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Harbour",
          tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],">="&R2,
          tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],"<"&S2)
```

(Type it on one line in Excel; it is split here only for reading.)

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Excel's Histogram chart draws its bins the other way round
In many Excel versions the built-in Histogram chart labels its bins as
$(400, 500]$: the **upper** bound belongs to the class. Our convention is
$[400, 500[$. With revenue to the cent a value of exactly 500.00 is rare,
but a number such as 500 or 600 *can* occur in other data. When in
doubt, trust your `COUNTIFS` table, not the chart labels. The PivotTable
grouping follows our convention (a value of exactly 500 goes into the
class starting at 500).
:::


### Step 0 — check your class results

1. Type the five revenues 600, 470, 730, 550 and 430 in `A2:A6`, and
   the class bounds in `C2:C5` (lower: 400, 500, 600, 700) and `D2:D5`
   (upper: 500, 600, 700, 800).
2. In `E2`, type `=COUNTIFS($A$2:$A$6,">="&C2,$A$2:$A$6,"<"&D2)` and
   copy it down to `E5`.
3. In `F2`, type `=E2` and in `F3` type `=F2+E3`, then copy down;
   in `G2`, type `=F2/COUNT($A$2:$A$6)`, formatted as a percentage,
   and copy down.
4. Compare every result with your hand computation.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Expected results</summary>

| Class (€) | $n_i$ | $N_i^{+}$ | $F_i^{+}$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| [400, 500[ | 2 | 2 | 40 |
| [500, 600[ | 1 | 3 | 60 |
| [600, 700[ | 1 | 4 | 80 |
| [700, 800[ | 1 | 5 | 100 |

Day 1 (exactly 600) is counted in [600, 700[, as expected from the
`>=` and `<` conditions.

</details>

### Homework 1 (Excel) — A skewed distribution

In `wandering-fork.xlsx`, build a class table for the **Campus**
`daily_revenue_eur` over all 120 days with classes of width 200 starting
at 0. Use `COUNTIFS` on `tblFork`. Add relative and cumulative
frequencies. What share of days earned less than €600, and how does the
shape differ from Harbour's?

**How to.** Copy the `COUNTIFS` formula from *Using Excel* and add the
condition `tblFork[franchise],"Campus"`.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

The formula for the class in row 2 is:

```text
=COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Campus",
          tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],">="&R2,
          tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],"<"&S2)
```

You should obtain:

| Class (€) | $n_i$ | $N_i^{+}$ | $f_i$ (%) | $F_i^{+}$ (%) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [0, 200[ | 25 | 25 | 20.8 | 20.8 |
| [200, 400[ | 37 | 62 | 30.8 | 51.7 |
| [400, 600[ | 30 | 92 | 25.0 | 76.7 |
| [600, 800[ | 11 | 103 | 9.2 | 85.8 |
| [800, 1000[ | 9 | 112 | 7.5 | 93.3 |
| [1000, 1200[ | 5 | 117 | 4.2 | 97.5 |
| [1200, 1400[ | 2 | 119 | 1.7 | 99.2 |
| [1400, 1600[ | 1 | 120 | 0.8 | 100.0 |

**76.7%** of Campus days earned less than €600. The tallest class is
[200, 400[ (37 days), and more than three days in four sit below €600,
but eight days (6.7%) earned €1,000 or more, up to €1,407.59. The
histogram has a tall peak on the left and a **long tail to the right**.
Harbour's revenue is more compact, with only a mild tail. We will give
this shape a name in Module 7.

</details>

### Homework 2 (Excel) — Group with a PivotTable

Using all 120 **Harbour** days, build the class table with a PivotTable
that groups `daily_revenue_eur` from 0 to 1,100 by steps of 100. What
share of days earned between €500 and €700?

**How to.** Filter `franchise` = Harbour, then right-click a row →
**Group**.

<details class="answer">
<summary>Solution</summary>

Filter `franchise` = Harbour, put `daily_revenue_eur` in
**Rows** and `day` in **Values** (set to *Count*), then right-click →
**Group** (*Starting at* 0, *Ending at* 1100, *By* 100). The counts
are:

| Class (€) | 0–99 | 100–199 | 200–299 | 300–399 | 400–499 | 500–599 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Days | 9 | 11 | 17 | 24 | 21 | 10 |

| Class (€) | 600–699 | 700–799 | 800–899 | 900–999 | 1000–1099 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Days | 16 | 7 | 3 | 0 | 2 |

They add up to 120 (the PivotTable does not show the empty 900–999
group). Days between €500 and €700 are the classes 500–599 and
600–699: $(10 + 16)/120 = 21.7\%$.

</details>
